column2: Stored XSS saves malicious script server-side (like a comment) and serves it to every viewer; reflected XSS bounces script off a URL parameter back into the response; DOM-based XSS happens client-side when JS writes untrusted data unsafely into the DOM (like `innerHTML = location.hash`). The primary defense for all three is context-aware output encoding at the point of use (escaping HTML special characters, keeping template autoescape on), which stops injected markup from being interpreted as executable script. CSP adds a second layer by restricting where scripts can load from and blocking inline script, so even if encoding is missed somewhere, an injected script often still can't execute.

column1: **Why is a token-auth API using `Authorization: Bearer` inherently more CSRF-resistant than cookie sessions, and what two defenses protect cookie sessions?**
column2: A Bearer-token API is inherently more CSRF-resistant because browsers don't auto-attach `Authorization` headers to cross-site requests the way they auto-attach cookies, so a malicious site can't forge a request carrying the victim's token. Cookie sessions need two explicit defenses: `SameSite=Strict/Lax` cookies (blocking the cookie from being sent on cross-site requests in the common case), and a synchronizer anti-CSRF token that the server requires in a header or field on state-changing requests, which a cross-origin attacker can't read due to the same-origin policy.

column1: **Explain SSRF: why can the server reach things the attacker can't, and what's the canonical high-value target on a cloud VM?**
column2: SSRF happens when the app fetches a URL the attacker controls, and the server has network access the attacker doesn't, it's inside the perimeter, able to reach internal-only services and cloud infrastructure that aren't exposed to the public internet. The canonical high-value target is the cloud metadata endpoint `169.254.169.254`, which on many cloud VMs serves IAM credentials to anything running locally; hitting it via SSRF can hand an attacker the server's own cloud permissions.

column1: **`allow_origins=["*"]` with `allow_credentials=True`, why is this dangerous, and what does it effectively undo?**
column2: This combination is dangerous (and disallowed by the CORS spec) because it would let any website read authenticated responses from your API on behalf of a logged-in victim, since credentials (cookies or auth headers) would be sent along with a request from literally any origin. It effectively undoes the browser's Same-Origin Policy, the core protection that a page can't read responses from a different origin; the fix is an explicit allowlist of trusted origins.

column1: **Why is testing only against a self-owned local target (and using a signed scope for anything else) non-negotiable, and what makes Juice Shop in Docker the right practice target?**
column2: Testing a system you don't own or have explicit written authorization to test can be a crime under laws like the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, even if nothing was technically "broken," so the only safe and legal targets are ones you own or have signed scope for. OWASP Juice Shop in Docker is the right practice target because it runs entirely on your own machine, you own it outright, there's no other person's data or system involved, and it's deliberately built with realistic vulnerabilities to practice recognizing and fixing.

column1: **Why does intercepting HTTPS require installing Burp's CA cert, which trust store does each browser use, and what real-world defense (in your own apps) makes this kind of interception hard for an actual attacker?**
column2: To intercept HTTPS, Burp has to decrypt the TLS in transit, which means acting as a consented, local man-in-the-middle, and browsers only trust certificates signed by a CA in their trust store, so you must install Burp's CA cert to make the browser accept its on-the-fly certificates. Firefox uses its own internal trust store (Settings → Certificates → Authorities), while Chrome, Edge, and Safari use the OS trust store (macOS Keychain, Windows Trusted Root store, Linux's `update-ca-certificates`). In your own apps, the real defense that makes this kind of interception hard for an actual attacker is that they'd need to already control the victim's device or trick them into installing their own CA; HSTS and certificate pinning further resist downgrade and substitution attacks.

column1: **Client-side form validation looks fine in the browser, but an intercepting proxy bypasses it. What does this prove about where security must be enforced?**
column2: This proves that security must be enforced on the server, never trusted from the client alone. Client-side JavaScript validation is UX, not security, since it's fully under the attacker's control; an intercepting proxy sends the server whatever raw HTTP a malicious client would send, bypassing the browser's checks entirely, so if the server still accepts an invalid or malicious value, the "protection" was never real.

column1: **Walk the Proxy→Repeater→Decoder→Comparer pipeline on the Juice Shop login/basket flow, and for each tool name the 12.3 defense the observation pointed to.**
column2: Proxy captured the raw `POST /rest/user/login` and showed the token comes back in the response body with no visible rate limit, pointing to A07 (add rate limiting/lockout on auth). Repeater replayed the login with edits, resending it rapidly with no throttle confirmed the missing rate limit, again A07. Decoder Base64-decoded the JWT's middle segment and showed readable claims including `role`, pointing to A02/A07 (verify the signature server-side, never trust a client-changed role claim). Comparer diffed an authorized basket response against a tampered-ID basket response and the difference proved cross-user data access, pointing to A01 broken access control (fix with server-side ownership scoping plus RLS).

column1: **Walk the Repeater workflow for confirming an IDOR, and state the exact server-side fix (and the defense-in-depth DB control).**
column2: Log in as user A, capture the request that loads A's own basket, send it to Repeater and confirm a baseline 200 with A's data, then change the basket ID in the path to a neighboring value while keeping A's token, and resend. If the server returns a different basket that isn't A's, that's confirmed IDOR. The exact fix is scoping the query server-side to the authenticated owner, `WHERE id = :basket_id AND owner_id = :current_user`, returning 404 otherwise, with Postgres Row-Level Security as the defense-in-depth database control that makes cross-tenant reads physically impossible even if the app-level check has a bug.

column1: **How would you turn your manual Burp checks into an automated, unattended guarantee, what runs in CI, and what stays interactive, and why?**
column2: You turn manual checks into automated regressions by scripting them: hit your own app directly with `httpx`/pytest to assert 401 on missing auth, 404 on IDOR attempts, presence of security headers like CSP and HSTS, and that CORS doesn't reflect an arbitrary Origin, or write a mitmproxy addon that asserts the same properties over real HTTP traffic. What runs in CI is that pytest/mitmproxy assertion suite, wired to fail the build the moment a security regression appears. What stays interactive is exploratory testing in Burp itself, manually probing new features or unusual inputs, because that's where you discover the checks worth automating in the first place.

column1: **You decode an auth token and can read a `role: user` claim. Why is that fine *if* one thing is true server-side, and what's the dangerous assumption that turns it into a vulnerability?**
column2: A readable `role: user` claim is fine as long as the server actually verifies the JWT's signature before trusting any claim in it, since JWTs are signed, not encrypted, so being readable doesn't by itself compromise anything. The dangerous assumption that turns it into a vulnerability is the server trusting a client-supplied or client-tampered `role` claim without checking the signature, or accepting an `alg: none` token, which lets an attacker rewrite `role` to `admin`, re-encode it, and get treated as an administrator with no valid signature required.

column1: **Derive the derivative of `x²` from the limit definition**, explaining why the `0/0` resolves.
column2: `f'(x) = lim_{h→0} ((x+h)² - x²)/h`. Expanding gives `(x² + 2xh + h² - x²)/h = (2xh + h²)/h`, and factoring h from the numerator and canceling (legal because h≠0 while approaching, not equal to it) leaves `2x + h`. Only now, with no h in the denominator, can you safely let h→0, getting `f'(x) = 2x`. The `0/0` resolves because the limit only cares about what the ratio approaches as h sneaks toward 0, not what happens exactly at h=0; algebraic cancellation removes the problematic h from the denominator before you ever plug in 0.

column1: **State the chain rule and explain why it *is* backpropagation**, rates multiply along the chain; a deep net is a deep composition.
column2: The chain rule is `d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))·g'(x)`, rates multiply along a chain: if u depends on x and y depends on u, then `dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx)`. A neural network is a deeply nested composition, loss of activation of weights of activation of weights of ... input, so finding how the loss changes with respect to a weight buried many layers deep means applying the chain rule once per layer, multiplying local derivatives together. Backpropagation is exactly this, organized so each local derivative is computed once and reused (dynamic programming on the computation graph), which is also why sigmoid's small derivative (≤0.25) compounding across many layers causes vanishing gradients while ReLU's derivative of 1 on the active path doesn't.

column1: **Explain why the gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent**, using the dot-product/cosine argument.
column2: To first order, stepping a unit distance v from point x changes f by `Δf ≈ ∇f · v = ‖∇f‖‖v‖cosθ = ‖∇f‖cosθ`, where θ is the angle between the step direction and the gradient. This change is maximized when `cosθ = 1`, i.e. θ=0, meaning v points exactly along ∇f, so among all possible step directions the gradient is the one that increases f the most. Stepping the opposite way (θ=180°, cosθ=-1) decreases f the most, that's gradient descent.

column1: **Write the gradient-descent update rule** and explain the role of the minus sign and the learning rate, in terms of the foggy hillside.
column2: The update rule is `x_{t+1} = x_t - η·f'(x_t)`, where η is the learning rate. The minus sign matters because f'(x) points uphill (toward increasing f), and since you want to decrease f, you step in the opposite direction, exactly the foggy hillside picture: feel the slope under your feet and step downhill against it. The learning rate η controls the step size: too small and convergence crawls, too large and you overshoot the valley and oscillate or diverge entirely.

column1: **State the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus** and give the "area-so-far function has the curve as its derivative" intuition for why differentiation and integration are inverses.
column2: The Fundamental Theorem states `∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) - F(a)` where `F' = f`: to find accumulated area under a rate, find an antiderivative and subtract its endpoints. The intuition: let F(x) be the accumulated area from a up to x; pushing the right edge x rightward by a tiny amount dx adds a sliver of area with height f(x) and width dx, so `dF ≈ f(x)dx`, meaning `dF/dx = f(x)`. The area-so-far function's derivative is the original function itself, which is exactly why differentiation and integration are inverse operations, accumulating and rate-of-change are two sides of one coin.

column1: **Explain convex vs. non-convex** and why it's the line between "optimization solved" and "optimization is an art", tying linear regression vs. deep nets.
column2: A function is convex if `f''(x) ≥ 0` everywhere (curves up like a cup); convexity guarantees exactly one minimum, and any local minimum is automatically the global minimum, so gradient descent is guaranteed to find the best answer. Non-convex functions can have many local minima and saddle points, so gradient descent might get stuck somewhere that isn't globally optimal. Linear and logistic regression have convex losses and train reliably to a unique optimum, while deep neural nets have wildly non-convex losses full of local minima and saddles, needing momentum, careful initialization, and learning-rate schedules to navigate, convex vs non-convex is literally the dividing line between "optimization is solved" and "optimization is an art."

column1: **Implement, from scratch, numerical differentiation (central difference), gradient descent on a 2D function, and the trapezoid rule**, then check each against SymPy's exact answer. Cross-links: complexity of these iterations (01.4), the discrete-sum foundations behind integration-as-summation (01.3), the statistics where integrals become probabilities (16.1), the linear algebra that makes gradients into vectors and the Hessian into a matrix (18.2), and the full backpropagation derivation this chapter sets up (14.2).
column2: Central difference approximates a derivative as `(f(x+h) - f(x-h))/(2h)`, more accurate than the forward difference because its error is O(h²) instead of O(h), and it's the standard way to sanity-check an analytic gradient by comparing it to this numerical estimate. A 2D gradient-descent loop computes the gradient at the current point, steps against it scaled by a learning rate, and repeats until convergence, exactly the loop used to train a linear regression by minimizing MSE. The trapezoid rule approximates a definite integral by summing trapezoids under the curve (`h·(0.5·y₀ + 0.5·y_n + Σ interior y)`), and all three should be checked against SymPy's exact symbolic results (`sp.diff`, `sp.integrate`) to confirm the numerical approximations converge to the same answer.

column1: **Explain what a matrix *does* to space**, columns are where the basis vectors land; it rotates/scales/shears/projects. Draw the cat-on-graph-paper.
column2: A matrix isn't just a grid of numbers, it's a function that transforms vectors, rotating, scaling, shearing, projecting, or flipping the space they live in. The key fact: a matrix's columns are exactly where the basis vectors (î and ĵ in 2D) land after the transformation, so applying the matrix to any vector `[x,y]` is a weighted sum of the columns, `x·(column 1) + y·(column 2)`. Picture graph paper with a cat drawn on it: the matrix is an operation on the whole sheet; spinning, stretching, or shearing the paper drags the cat's outline, and every vector on the sheet, along with it.

column1: **Derive matrix multiplication as composition**, `AB` means "do `B`, then `A`," which is why it's non-commutative and why dimensions must match.
column2: `AB` means "do B first, then A," you're finding a single matrix C such that `Cv = A(Bv)` for all v. Because column j of C is where basis vector j lands after applying B and then A, working that out entry by entry gives the familiar rule `C_ij = Σ_k A_ik B_kj`, row i of A dotted with column j of B. It's non-commutative because "rotate then shear" is a genuinely different transformation from "shear then rotate," order matters; dimensions must match (A is m×n, B is n×p) because B's output has to be a valid input for A.

column1: **Explain the dot product two ways** (sum of products *and* `‖a‖‖b‖cos θ`) and why it's a similarity score, connecting to cosine similarity and embeddings.
column2: The dot product is `a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ` (sum of products) and also `‖a‖‖b‖cosθ` (magnitude times the cosine of the angle between them); the two formulas are equal, which is what makes the dot product a similarity score: same direction gives a large positive value, perpendicular gives zero, opposite gives a large negative value. Cosine similarity is just the dot product normalized by both vectors' lengths, isolating the angle and ignoring magnitude, which is exactly why embeddings (words, documents, images) are compared by cosine similarity, two embeddings pointing the same way mean similar content regardless of vector length.

column1: **Explain the determinant as area scaling** and why `det = 0` ⟺ non-invertible (a destroyed dimension can't be recovered).
column2: The determinant answers "by what factor does this transformation scale area (or volume)?" `det=2` doubles all areas, `det=1` preserves area (rotations), `det=0` collapses space onto a lower dimension, squashing area to zero. A destroyed dimension can't be recovered: if det=0, infinitely many different inputs map to the same output, so there's no way to reverse the transformation, which is exactly why `det(A)≠0` is equivalent to A being invertible.

column1: **Derive eigenvalues** from `Av = λv` → `(A−λI)v = 0` → `det(A−λI) = 0`, and explain what an eigenvector *means* (an invariant direction the transform only scales).
column2: Rearranging `Av = λv` gives `(A - λI)v = 0`, which says the nonzero vector v gets mapped to zero by `(A - λI)`; a matrix can only crush a nonzero vector to zero if it's singular, so `det(A - λI) = 0`, the characteristic equation. Expanding this determinant gives a polynomial whose roots are the eigenvalues; solving `(A - λI)v = 0` for each root gives the corresponding eigenvector. An eigenvector is an invariant direction, a direction the transformation only stretches or shrinks (by the eigenvalue λ) without rotating off its own line, the axes the transformation is "built around."

column1: **Implement power iteration** and explain why it finds the dominant eigenvector, connect to PageRank.
column2: Power iteration repeatedly applies A to a random vector and renormalizes each step: `v ← Av/‖Av‖`. It converges to the dominant eigenvector because writing the starting vector in the eigenvector basis, each application of A scales each component by its own eigenvalue, so after k applications the component along the largest-magnitude eigenvector dominates while every other component's relative contribution shrinks as `(λᵢ/λ₁)^k → 0`. This is literally how Google's original PageRank works: the web is a giant link matrix, and the dominant eigenvector of that matrix is the stationary distribution of a random surfer, i.e. PageRank.

column1: **State SVD** (`A = UΣVᵀ` = rotate-scale-rotate) and why truncating it gives optimal compression, connect to image compression and recommenders.
column2: SVD factors any matrix as `A = UΣVᵀ`, meaning every linear transformation is a rotation, then a scaling along axes (the singular values, sorted largest first), then another rotation. Truncating to the top k singular values gives the best possible rank-k approximation of A (the Eckart-Young theorem), because the singular values measure how much "energy" or variance lives along each direction, and the small ones discarded carry little information. This is why image compression works (an image is a matrix; keep the top singular values and most of the visual structure survives) and why recommender systems work (a user×item ratings matrix is approximately low-rank, a few latent "taste" factors explain most ratings).

column1: **Derive PCA as the eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix** via the maximum-variance / Lagrange-multiplier argument, and implement it from scratch. Cross-links: the dot products and gradients of 18.1 (the steepest-ascent proof was a dot product; the Hessian is a matrix), the covariance and variance of 16.1 (PCA is built on the covariance matrix), the complexity of these operations, matrix multiply is `O(n³)` naïvely (01.4), the discrete structures underneath (01.3), and the embeddings and PCA used throughout ML (14.1) and as inputs to neural nets (14.2). Together, 18.1 and 18.2 are the mathematical bedrock the entire ML stack stands on, gradients to optimize, vectors and matrices to compute, eigenvalues to find the structure in data. No more black boxes.
column2: PCA finds the unit direction w that maximizes the variance of the projected, centered data, `Var(Xw) = wᵀCw` subject to `‖w‖=1`, where C is the covariance matrix. Setting the gradient of the Lagrangian `wᵀCw - λ(wᵀw - 1)` to zero gives `Cw = λw`, exactly the eigenvector equation, so the direction of maximum variance is the eigenvector of the covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalue, and that eigenvalue equals the variance captured along it. Implementing it from scratch means: center the data, compute the covariance matrix, eigendecompose it (`np.linalg.eigh` since C is symmetric), sort eigenvectors by eigenvalue descending, and project onto the top k eigenvectors, matching scikit-learn's PCA exactly (up to a sign flip).

column1: **What is a rational agent, and why is "rational" different from "successful" and from "omniscient"?**
column2: A rational agent, for each possible percept sequence, selects an action expected to maximize its performance measure, given its built-in knowledge and what it has perceived so far. It's different from "successful" because rationality is about making the best decision given available information, not about guaranteeing a good outcome, a rational poker player can play perfectly and still lose a hand. It's different from "omniscient" because you can only be rational about what you could have known; an agent that couldn't have foreseen an outcome wasn't irrational for not avoiding it.

column1: **Frame "find the cheapest route" as a search problem** (all five components). Which uninformed search is optimal, and under what condition?
column2: The five components are: initial state (starting location), actions (legal moves from a location), a transition model/result function (where an action leads), a goal test (is this the destination), and a step cost (the price of each move, e.g. distance). Uniform-Cost Search (Dijkstra-style, ordering the frontier by accumulated path cost) is optimal for any non-negative step costs, always expanding the cheapest path so far. BFS is only optimal under the special condition that every step cost is equal, since it finds the shallowest goal, which equals cheapest only when depth is proportional to cost.

column1: **Why is A\* optimal?** State admissibility and consistency, and give the one-line argument for each.
column2: A* is optimal because with an admissible heuristic, any node n still on the optimal path always has `f(n) = g(n)+h(n) ≤ C*` (the optimal cost), while a suboptimal goal G₂ has `f(G₂) = g(G₂) > C*`, so A* always expands the optimal-path node before it could return the suboptimal goal. Admissibility means the heuristic never overestimates the true cost-to-go (`h(n) ≤ h*(n)`), it's optimistic. Consistency is the stronger triangle-inequality property (`h(n) ≤ cost(n,a,n') + h(n')`) that guarantees f never decreases along any path, so a state is never re-expanded once popped.

column1: **Why does a "more informed" admissible heuristic never hurt**, and where do good heuristics come from?
column2: A more-informed (larger but still admissible) heuristic dominates a weaker one, meaning it expands no more nodes, because a tighter, still-optimistic estimate lets A* prune more aggressively without ever risking overestimating and missing the optimal solution. Good heuristics usually come from relaxing the problem: solving an easier version where some constraint is removed (like letting 8-puzzle tiles pass through each other, giving Manhattan distance) gives a cost that's always an admissible estimate for the real, harder problem.

column1: **Walk through minimax**, then explain what alpha-beta prunes and why the answer is *unchanged*.
column2: Minimax assumes a perfect opponent: at a MAX node it takes the maximum of children's backed-up values, at a MIN node the minimum, all the way down to terminal states whose true utility is known, then backs those values up through alternating min/max layers so the root picks the move leading to the best guaranteed outcome. Alpha-beta pruning carries two bounds down the recursion, α (the best MAX can already guarantee) and β (the best MIN can already guarantee), and prunes any subtree where `α ≥ β` because that branch can no longer influence the final decision. The answer is unchanged because pruning never discards a branch that could actually change the backed-up value at the root, it's a pure efficiency optimization, not an approximation.

column1: **Why is tic-tac-toe with optimal play always a draw**, but chess engines use evaluation functions instead of searching to the end?
column2: Tic-tac-toe with optimal play always draws because minimax exhaustively proves that neither player can force a win against a perfect opponent, the game tree is small enough to search completely to terminal states. Chess engines use evaluation functions instead because chess's game tree (~10^40 states) is far too deep to search to terminal states in any reasonable time, so engines cut off the search at a depth limit and estimate who's winning with a hand-crafted or learned evaluation function rather than knowing the true outcome.

column1: **What is a CSP**, and what do AC-3 and MRV each buy you?
column2: A CSP is variables with domains of allowed values, plus constraints restricting which value combinations are legal, like Sudoku, map coloring, or scheduling. AC-3 (arc consistency propagation) buys you pruning: it deletes values that can't possibly participate in any solution before or during search, often solving easy instances with zero backtracking. MRV (Minimum Remaining Values, assign the most-constrained variable next) buys you failing fast: if a variable is about to run out of legal values, you discover that immediately instead of many levels deeper into a doomed branch.

column1: **What's entailment vs. inference**, and how does resolution prove something by refutation?
column2: Entailment (`KB ⊨ α`) means α is true in every world where the knowledge base is true; inference is the mechanical process of actually deriving entailed sentences from the KB. Resolution proves entailment by refutation: to show `KB ⊨ α`, you add `¬α` to the KB and repeatedly apply the resolution rule (from `(A∨B)` and `(¬A∨C)` infer `(B∨C)`) until you derive the empty clause, a contradiction, which proves the KB together with the negated query is unsatisfiable, meaning the original query must be entailed.

column1: **Why did learning beat hand-coding** for perception, and where is hand-coded/symbolic AI still the *right* choice? ---
column2: Learning beat hand-coding for perception because problems like vision and speech defied rule-writing, nobody can articulate the rules for "is this a cat," while statistical/deep learning infers those rules from data instead of demanding humans state them, and it degrades gracefully on noisy or off-distribution input where symbolic systems fail brittle and total. Hand-coded/symbolic AI is still the right choice for crisp, well-defined problems needing guarantees, chess, Sudoku, scheduling, theorem proving, constraint solvers running logistics or chip verification, anywhere correctness and transparency matter more than handling messy perceptual input.

column1: **Why is a production ML system fundamentally harder to operate than ordinary software?** (Silent failure, data dependence, decay.)
column2: Three things make it harder: production ML systems fail silently, a model that's quietly become less accurate throws nothing, no 500, no page, it just keeps returning confident wrong answers until a business metric tanks. They depend on data, not just code, so "reproducible" now means version-pinning data too, and a bug can live entirely in the data pipeline while the code stays untouched. And they rot: even a perfect model decays as the world drifts away from its training data, so a model isn't a deliverable you ship once, it's a service you keep alive with monitoring and retraining.

column1: **What is data leakage?** Name three forms and the discipline that prevents each.
column2: Data leakage is when information that wouldn't be available at prediction time sneaks into training, inflating the offline score in a way that collapses in production. Target leakage is a feature that's a proxy for the label itself (like `account_closed_date` when predicting churn), prevented by auditing each feature for "is this knowable at prediction time?" Train/test contamination is fitting a scaler or encoder on the full dataset before splitting, prevented by always using a `Pipeline` so preprocessing re-fits on train only, inside each CV fold. Temporal leakage is using future information to predict the past, prevented by splitting time-series data by time (`TimeSeriesSplit`), never randomly.

column1: **Why is accuracy usually the wrong metric**, and what do you use instead for imbalanced problems? Why PR-AUC over ROC-AUC?
column2: Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data because a trivial "always predict the majority class" model can score extremely high (99.5% accurate on 0.5% fraud) while being useless. Instead use precision, recall, and F1, and choose the operating threshold from the business cost asymmetry rather than the default 0.5. PR-AUC is preferred over ROC-AUC on rare-positive problems because ROC-AUC can look great while the model is actually useless on the rare class (dominated by the huge number of true negatives), while PR-AUC directly reflects performance on the positives you actually care about.

column1: **What is slicing and why is it non-negotiable** for both quality and fairness?
column2: Slicing means evaluating model performance separately on meaningful subgroups (new users, a region, a device type) instead of just one global average metric. It's non-negotiable for quality because a model can be 95% accurate overall but 60% accurate on a subgroup that matters, and a global metric averages that failure away, hiding it until it costs the business. It's non-negotiable for fairness because the same averaging can hide discriminatory behavior against a demographic or protected group, and you can't fix or even see a problem you never measured.

column1: **Explain gradient boosting as "gradient descent in function space."** What does each tree fit, and what does XGBoost add?
column2: Gradient boosting builds an additive model stage by stage, and at each stage the new tree is fit to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions, the direction that would most reduce the loss; for squared error that negative gradient is exactly the residual, so each tree predicts the current errors and gets added in to nudge predictions toward the truth, one small step downhill on the loss surface, with the learning rate as step size. XGBoost adds a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss (using the Hessian, not just the gradient, for better steps), explicit regularization on tree complexity to resist overfitting, and fast, sparsity-aware split-finding.

column1: **Data drift vs. concept drift**, which can you detect *without* labels, and how (PSI)?
column2: Data drift (covariate shift) is when the input distribution `P(X)` changes, the model was trained on a world that no longer exists; concept drift is when the relationship `P(Y|X)` changes, the same inputs now mean a different outcome, more dangerous and usually needing labels (eventually) to detect. Data drift can be detected in real time without labels by comparing the live feature distribution to the training distribution, using the Population Stability Index (PSI); a rule of thumb is PSI under 0.1 is stable, 0.1-0.25 is moderate shift, and above 0.25 is significant drift worth investigating.

column1: **Walk shadow → canary → A/B.** What does each one buy you, and why do ML models especially need careful rollout?
column2: Shadow deployment runs the new model on real production traffic in parallel without acting on its output, just logging and comparing, buying zero-risk validation that it behaves sanely and meets latency budgets. Canary routes a small, growing slice of traffic to the new model with automatic rollback if metrics degrade, buying limited blast radius. A/B testing deliberately splits traffic to measure the actual business metric with statistical significance, buying the ground-truth online evaluation that an offline metric can't provide. ML models especially need careful rollout because they fail silently, a model that looks better offline can be worse online in ways the offline metric never showed.

column1: **What is CT (continuous training)**, and what *extra* things does an ML CI pipeline test beyond code?
column2: CT (Continuous Training) is the automated pipeline that retrains, re-evaluates, and re-deploys a model on a trigger, the full lifecycle running as a self-sustaining loop rather than a manual notebook run. Beyond testing code, an ML CI pipeline also validates data (schema checks, distribution checks, no unexpected nulls) and runs model tests: does the new model beat a baseline on a frozen eval set, does it pass behavioral invariance tests, and does it hold up on every slice, so a model that improves overall but tanks a protected slice fails the pipeline.

column1: **What four things must you version** to make a model reproducible, and why is data the one people miss?
column2: You must version code (a git SHA), data (a version or hash, what tools like DVC handle), environment (pinned dependencies or a Docker image), and config/hyperparameters (tracked per run); pin all four and any model is rebuildable byte-for-byte. Data is the one people miss because `git` naturally tracks code but not the datasets a model was trained on, and "works on my machine" is fatal in ML precisely because the model depends on data you can't see in your code repository, miss that one piece and nobody can reproduce or debug the model months later.

column1: **What goes in a model card vs. a runbook**, and why is "how to roll back" the most important runbook section? ---
column2: A model card documents intended use and out-of-scope uses, the training data and its known limitations/biases, evaluation metrics including the sliced breakdown, the chosen threshold and why, and known failure modes, aimed at understanding what the model is and isn't good for. A runbook is operational: how to tell if the model is healthy, what each alert means and the first things to check, how to trigger a retrain, and who owns it. "How to roll back" is the most important runbook section because a model without a documented, fast rollback path isn't production-ready, it's a liability with a confidence score, since it's the one action that bounds the worst-case damage when something goes wrong at 3 a.m.

column1: **One sentence:** an LLM is a next-token predictor; doing that well over all of text forces it to learn structure, and generation is just prediction run in a loop.
column2: An LLM is a next-token predictor, trained to assign a probability distribution over what token comes next given everything before it; doing that well across the entire span of human text forces the model to internalize grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns as a side effect of the prediction objective, and generation is just that prediction run repeatedly in a loop, each output token appended and fed back in.

column1: **Tokenization:** text → subword tokens via BPE (merge frequent adjacent pairs); the model never sees characters (hence spelling errors), and cost/context are measured in tokens (~4 chars each).
column2: Text is converted to subword tokens via Byte-Pair Encoding, which starts with every character as its own token and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair, so common words become single tokens while rare words get split into pieces. Because the model operates on token IDs, not characters, it never truly "sees" individual letters, which is why it can miscount the r's in "strawberry." Cost and context windows are measured in tokens, not words, roughly ~4 characters or ~1.3 tokens per English word, so a prompt looks shorter in words than it actually costs in tokens.

column1: **Embeddings:** tokens → vectors where meaning is direction; similarity = cosine of the angle (ties to 18.2's dot product).
column2: Each token maps to a learned vector in a high-dimensional embedding space, and meaning becomes geometry: tokens used in similar ways end up pointing in similar directions. Similarity between two vectors is measured as the cosine of the angle between them, the dot product normalized by both lengths (ties directly to 18.2's `a·b = ‖a‖‖b‖cosθ`), which isolates direction and ignores magnitude, exactly what semantic search and RAG retrieval rank by.

column1: **Attention:** `softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V`, each token's query matches every key to weight a blend of values; `√dₖ` prevents gradient saturation; causal masking forbids looking ahead; multi-head = several lenses in parallel; positional encoding restores word order.
column2: Attention computes `softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V`: each token's query is dotted against every token's key to get relevance scores, softmax turns those into weights summing to 1, and the output is a weighted blend of all tokens' values, so a token gathers context from wherever it's relevant. Dividing by `√dₖ` prevents the dot products from growing large enough to saturate softmax and kill gradients. Causal masking zeroes out future positions so a token predicting the next word can't peek ahead. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel with different learned projections, each head potentially tracking a different kind of relationship, and since attention itself is order-blind, positional encoding is added to restore word order.

column1: **Training:** pretraining (next-token, huge scale) → SFT (instruction demos) → RLHF/DPO (human preferences). Scaling laws make bigger runs predictably better.
column2: Pretraining trains a decoder-only network on next-token prediction over a massive corpus, giving a base model with broad knowledge and fluency but no assistant behavior. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) then fine-tunes on curated (prompt, ideal response) pairs, turning a text-completer into an instruction-follower. RLHF or DPO aligns the model to human preferences by ranking multiple responses and optimizing toward the ones humans prefer, teaching tone, refusals, and formatting that's cheaper to scale than hand-writing perfect answers for everything. Scaling laws describe loss falling predictably as model size, data, and compute increase together, which is why bigger, well-balanced runs reliably buy better capabilities.

column1: **Decoding:** greedy vs sampling; temperature (randomness), top-k/top-p (candidate set). Low temp for JSON/facts.
column2: Greedy decoding always picks the highest-probability token, deterministic but repetitive; sampling draws randomly from the distribution, more diverse but riskier. Temperature rescales logits before softmax: low temperature sharpens the distribution toward argmax (deterministic, focused), high temperature flattens it (more random, more creative and error-prone). Top-k keeps only the k most probable tokens before sampling; top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, adapting the candidate pool to the model's confidence. For anything that must be correct or parseable, like JSON output, use low temperature since randomness adds noise, not knowledge.

column1: **Hallucinations:** the objective rewards plausibility, knowledge is frozen/lossy, and the model doesn't know what it doesn't know, mitigate with RAG, low temp, validation, and "say I don't know."
column2: Hallucinations happen because the training objective rewards plausible-sounding text, not verified truth, so a fabricated-but-plausible citation is exactly the kind of thing that "should" come next to the model. Training data has a cutoff and is lossily compressed into weights, and the model doesn't reliably know the boundary of its own knowledge, so it fills gaps with a confident best guess rather than admitting uncertainty. Mitigations: RAG (grounding in real source text is the biggest lever), lower temperature for factual tasks, instructing the model to cite sources or say "I don't know," and structured output with schema validation so malformed or implausible answers get caught before they're trusted.

column1: **Prompting:** system prompt, few-shot (in-context learning), chain-of-thought, structured JSON + validate + retry (your NYX pattern).
column2: The system prompt is a persistent instruction framing the model's role, constraints, and output format for the whole conversation. Few-shot prompting includes input→output examples so the model pattern-matches the demonstrated format through in-context learning, no weight updates needed. Chain-of-thought asks the model to reason step by step before answering, which measurably improves accuracy on multi-step problems because each reasoning token becomes context for the next. The structured JSON pattern specifies an exact schema, gives one or two valid examples, uses the provider's JSON mode if available, and validates the result against a schema like Pydantic, retrying with the error fed back if it fails.

column1: **RAG:** chunk → embed → vector index → cosine retrieve top-k → stuff context → grounded generate. Grounding is the biggest hallucination lever.
column2: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) grounds an LLM in external data it wasn't trained on: split documents into overlapping chunks, embed each chunk into a vector, store them in a vector index for fast nearest-neighbor search, then at query time embed the question and retrieve the top-k most similar chunks by cosine similarity, stuff those chunks into the prompt, and instruct the model to answer only from that context. Grounding is the biggest hallucination lever because it gives the model actual source text to answer from instead of relying on its frozen, lossy internal knowledge.

column1: **When to use what:** prompt first; RAG for knowledge; fine-tune for behavior at scale, and they compose. ---
column2: Start with prompting, it's cheapest and fastest to iterate, and most problems are actually prompt problems. Reach for RAG when the issue is knowledge, the model lacks facts or hallucinates, since RAG injects truth while fine-tuning generally doesn't reliably teach new facts. Reach for fine-tuning when the issue is behavior at scale, a very specific output style or format needed consistently, or thousands of examples that prompting can't fit. These aren't rivals, they compose: a fine-tuned model with RAG and a good system prompt is common in production.

column1: **Agent = LLM + tools + loop.** Perceive → reason → act → observe → repeat, with autonomy over *when* to act, *which* tool, and *when done*. Add autonomy only where the task needs it; a fixed workflow is often better.
column2: An agent is an LLM placed in a control loop where it can choose actions (tool calls) based on observations while pursuing a goal, cycling through perceive (read the goal and situation), reason (decide what's needed next), act (call a tool), observe (read the result), and repeat until done. The autonomy is specifically over when to act, which tool to use, and when the task is complete, that's what distinguishes an agent from a single LLM call. Autonomy should only be added where the task genuinely needs open-ended decision-making; a fixed workflow with the LLM filling in narrow pieces is often more reliable, cheaper, and easier to debug.

column1: **ReAct:** interleave Thought (reasoning) and Action (tool call), read the Observation, loop, bounded by max-steps. Externalize what the model is bad at (math, fresh facts, side effects) to tools.
column2: ReAct interleaves a Thought (chain-of-thought reasoning about what's needed next) with an Action (a tool call), reads the resulting Observation, and loops back to reasoning armed with that new information, continuing until the model produces a Final Answer, bounded by a max-steps guard so a confused agent can't loop forever. The key move is externalizing what the model is bad at, exact arithmetic, fresh facts, real-world side effects, to tools, while keeping the part it's good at, deciding what to do next, inside the model itself.

column1: **Function calling:** describe tools as JSON Schema → model picks a tool & args → **validate** → execute → feed result back. The schema/description is the contract; treat model output as untrusted.
column2: You describe each tool to the model as JSON Schema (name, description, typed parameters); the model, fine-tuned to recognize when a tool is appropriate, emits a structured tool-call choosing a tool and filling in arguments based on matching the tool's description to the need. The runtime then validates those arguments against the schema before ever executing, since model output is untrusted input, executes the tool in your own code, and feeds the result back to the model as an observation so it can continue. The schema and description are the contract that determines whether the model picks the right tool with valid arguments; write them carefully.

column1: **MCP:** Anthropic's 2024 standard (de-facto by 2026) that turns the M×N tool-integration mess into M+N, one JSON-Schema protocol for tools/resources/prompts across vendors. Write tools once, use everywhere.
column2: MCP (Model Context Protocol), introduced by Anthropic in 2024 and the de-facto standard by 2026, is a single JSON-Schema-based protocol for connecting models to tools, data resources, and reusable prompt templates. Before MCP every tool integration was bespoke glue code per model and per app, an M×N problem; MCP turns that into M+N because you write a tool once as an MCP server and any MCP-capable client or model can call it, no rewrites needed across frameworks or vendors.

column1: **Memory:** short-term (context) + long-term (vector store / RAG over history) + summarization to stay within the window.
column2: Short-term memory is the current transcript kept in the context window, fast but bounded and ephemeral. Long-term memory persists facts outside the context in a database or vector store and retrieves them when relevant, essentially RAG applied to the agent's own history, letting it "remember" things like a user's stated preferences across sessions. Summarization compacts older turns into a condensed note once the transcript grows too long, keeping the agent within its context budget while preserving the gist, though you have to watch for detail loss and keep critical facts verbatim.

column1: **Planning:** decomposition, task graphs (DAGs, parallelism, dependencies, LangGraph), reflection/self-critique. More power, more cost, match to the task. RAG becomes a tool the agent calls when it decides it needs to.
column2: Decomposition breaks a big goal into sub-tasks up front rather than deciding one step at a time. Task graphs represent those sub-tasks as a DAG so independent branches can run in parallel and dependencies are explicit, exactly what LangGraph models as state transitions. Reflection has the agent critique and revise its own output ("does this answer the question? is it grounded?"), which measurably improves quality on hard tasks at the cost of more tokens and latency. More planning and reflection means better results but more cost, so match the machinery to the task's actual difficulty. RAG becomes just one tool the agent can call when it decides it needs to look something up, rather than something always statically stuffed into context.

column1: **Multi-agent:** roles + orchestration (supervisor / conversational / pipeline). Helps for separable, parallel, specialized work; hurts on simple or tightly-coupled tasks (cost × N, compounding errors). Start single-agent.
column2: Multi-agent systems assign distinct roles (researcher, analyst, writer, critic) coordinated by an orchestration pattern, supervisor/worker delegation, conversational back-and-forth, or a fixed pipeline hand-off. They help when sub-tasks are genuinely separable, parallelizable, or benefit from role-specific prompts and tools, and when a critic agent catches errors a single agent would miss. They hurt on simple tasks (pure orchestration overhead) or tightly-coupled steps (agents pass garbled context and compound each other's errors), and cost multiplies by N agents while errors can compound rather than cancel. The default should be starting single-agent and only splitting into roles when you can name the specific benefit.

column1: **2026 frameworks:** LangGraph (explicit state, high control) → CrewAI (pre-assembled orchestration, fast) on the control spectrum; Claude Agent SDK (production, Anthropic-native), AutoGen (conversational), LlamaIndex (RAG-first), Pydantic AI (type-safe + FastAPI). All speak MCP.
column2: LangGraph sits at the high-control end, you explicitly define nodes and edges as a state graph, verbose but fully inspectable and debuggable, while CrewAI sits at the fast-prototyping end, pre-assembling role-based orchestration so you declare who and what and the framework handles the loop. The Claude Agent SDK is Anthropic-native and production-focused with the agent loop and MCP handled for you; AutoGen is built for conversational multi-agent patterns; LlamaIndex is RAG-first, best when the agent's core job is querying your data; Pydantic AI gives type-safe, FastAPI-style ergonomics. All of them speak MCP, so the tool layer you build is portable across whichever framework you choose.

column1: **Production:** evaluation (trajectory + success rate on golden tasks), guardrails (input/action/output), cost & runaway control (max steps, budgets, loop detection, timeouts), observability/tracing (13.1), security (prompt injection, sandboxing, least privilege, 12-Security), human-in-the-loop for consequential actions. ---
column2: Evaluating an agent means measuring task success rate on a golden set, trajectory quality (did it use the right tools efficiently or wander), and cost/latency per task, since an agent is a whole trajectory, not one output. Guardrails constrain input (reject malicious/off-topic requests), action (allow-list tools, require approval for dangerous ones, cap argument ranges), and output (validate schema, filter unsafe content). Cost and runaway control means hard limits: max steps, token/dollar budgets, loop detection, and timeouts. Observability/tracing means recording every thought, tool call, and observation so a failed run can be replayed and debugged. Security means treating prompt injection as the top threat, sandboxing any code execution, and applying least privilege so an agent only has the minimum tools and permissions its job needs. Human-in-the-loop puts a person in the approval path for consequential or irreversible actions, like anything that moves money or sends external communication, as the pragmatic safety net while autonomy matures.

column1: Derive why `a[i]` is O(1). Write the address formula, name every term (`base`, `i`, `stride`), and explain why the cost doesn't depend on `i` or on `n`. What property of the array makes this formula possible in the first place?
column2: The formula is `address(a[i]) = base_address + i * stride`, where `base_address` is where element 0 starts, `i` is the index, and `stride` is the number of bytes one element occupies. To read `a[i]` the CPU does one multiplication and one addition, then one memory fetch, a fixed handful of operations regardless of how large `i` or `n` is, so it qualifies as O(1) by definition (a cost that doesn't grow with input size). This is only possible because the array is **contiguous**: every element is the same size and laid end to end, so any element's address is a closed-form arithmetic expression rather than something you have to search for.

column1: A dynamic array is "a lie maintained on top of a fixed buffer." Explain the lie. What two numbers must the structure track, and what happens, step by step, when `append` is called and `size == capacity`?
column2: The lie is that a dynamic array looks infinitely growable, but underneath it is still a fixed-size contiguous block of memory; growth is faked by secretly swapping in a bigger buffer when needed. The structure tracks **capacity** (how big the underlying buffer actually is) and **size** (how many slots are currently filled). When `append` is called and `size == capacity`, `_resize` fires: a new, bigger buffer is allocated (`2 * capacity`, geometric growth), every existing element is copied into it, the old buffer is discarded, then the new value is written at `buffer[size]` and `size` is incremented.

column1: Prove that `append` is amortized O(1) using the aggregate method: show that the total copying cost over `n` appends with doubling sums to a geometric series, evaluate it to `≈ 2n`, and conclude the per-append cost. Then redo the proof with the accounting method (how many credits per append, and why does the bank never go negative?).
column2: Aggregate method: every append does one cheap write (n writes total), plus resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., so the copying totals `1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n ≈ 2n - 1 < 2n` (in a doubling series the last term beats everything before it combined). Total work is `≤ n + 2n = 3n`, so average cost per append is `3n / n = 3 = O(1)`. Accounting method: charge each `append` 3 credits, 1 to pay for the write and 2 banked with the element; right after a resize from `k` to `2k` the buffer is half full, so the next `k` appends deposit `2k` credits, exactly enough to pay for copying the `2k` elements at the next resize, meaning the bank never runs dry and the flat charge of 3 is always sufficient.

column1: Suppose you changed the growth strategy from "double the capacity" to "add 10 slots each time it fills." What does the amortized cost of `append` become, and why? Show the sum. (This is the question that proves you understand why doubling matters, not just that it's used.)
column2: The amortized cost degrades to O(n), and the total cost over `n` appends becomes O(n²). With additive growth by 10, resizes happen roughly every 10 appends, copying sizes `10 + 20 + 30 + ... + n`, which is an arithmetic series summing to about `n²/20`. Because each resize copies a growing amount and resizes don't get rarer relative to the copy size the way doubling's gaps do, the total is quadratic in `n`, so per-append cost is O(n) rather than O(1); the chapter's own example (growing by 1 slot each time) makes this explicit as `1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 = O(n²)`.

column1: Why are `insert(0, x)` and `delete(0)` both O(n) while `append` and `pop()` from the end are O(1)? Tie your answer directly to the contiguity invariant: what does contiguity force us to do when we open or close a gap in the middle?
column2: Contiguity means there are no gaps in the buffer, so opening a hole at index 0 for `insert` forces every element from `i` onward to physically slide one slot right, and closing a hole after `delete` forces every element after `i` to slide one slot left; at the front that's `n` (or `n-1`) shifts, hence O(n). `append` and `pop()` operate at the end where nobody is in the way, so no shifting is needed, just one write (or a decrement of `size`), which is O(1). The array is fast to read anywhere but fast to modify only at the end, exactly because contiguity has no slack for insertions except at the boundary.

column1: Python's `list` is a dynamic array. Using only what's in this chapter, predict the Big-O of: `lst[500]`, `lst.append(x)`, `lst.insert(0, x)`, `lst.pop()`, `lst.pop(0)`, and `x in lst`. For each, name the one-line reason. If you wanted fast inserts at the front, what should you reach for instead, and why?
column2: `lst[500]` is O(1): direct offset arithmetic, `base + i*stride`. `lst.append(x)` is O(1) amortized: geometric doubling makes resize copies sum to `< 2n` over `n` appends. `lst.insert(0, x)` is O(n): every element must shift right to open the gap at the front. `lst.pop()` is O(1): shrinking from the end just decrements `size`, no shifting. `lst.pop(0)` is O(n): every remaining element shifts left to close the gap. `x in lst` is O(n): unsorted, so it must scan linearly with no structure to exploit. For fast front inserts, reach for `collections.deque`, which is O(1) at both ends, unlike a contiguous array whose only cheap end is the back.

column1: **The mental model.** Sketch `3 → 7 → 9 → None` as nodes-with-pointers and explain, referencing the C++ `struct Node { int data; Node* next; };`, why `cur = cur->next` walks the list and why the nodes need not be adjacent in memory.
column2: Each node is `struct Node { int data; Node* next; }`, so the chain is three boxes: `{3, ●}→{7, ●}→{9, nullptr}`, where head points at the `3` node and each `●` is the address stored in `next`. `cur = cur->next` means "replace your hand-position with the address the current node is pointing at," so repeating it walks 3, then 7, then 9, stopping when `next` is `nullptr`. Because `next` stores an address rather than requiring physical placement, node `7` could live at `0x1000` and node `9` at `0x40`; the only thing linking them is that `7`'s `next` field literally holds `9`'s address, so the nodes never need to be adjacent in memory.

column1: **Derive the trade-off.** From first principles (not the table), prove why front-insertion is O(1) for a linked list but O(n) for an array, and why index access is the reverse. Then explain why, despite this, iterating an array is usually faster in practice - use the words "cache line" and "pointer chase."
column2: Front-insertion on a linked list is three pointer writes, new node's `next` set to the old head, then `head` reassigned, none of which depends on `n`, so it's O(1); on an array, contiguity means inserting at index 0 forces every one of the `n` existing elements to shift right, so it's O(n). Index access flips: an array computes `base + i*stride` directly, O(1), while a linked list has no arithmetic shortcut and must follow `next` from `head` exactly `i` times, O(n). Despite the list's O(1) front insert, arrays usually win in practice because the CPU pulls a whole **cache line** (about 64 bytes) at a time and an array's contiguous layout lets the prefetcher stream through those lines with near-zero misses, whereas walking a list is a **pointer chase** where each node is scattered on the heap and the next address isn't known until the current node is read, so nearly every hop risks a costly cache miss.

column1: **Reverse it.** Walk through reversing `1→2→3` with the three pointers `prev/cur/nxt`. Why must you stash `nxt = cur.next` before doing `cur.next = prev`? State the loop invariant and why it proves correctness.
column2: Starting `prev=None, cur=1`: save `nxt=cur.next` (2), flip `cur.next=prev` (1→None), advance `prev=1, cur=2`. Repeat: save `nxt=3`, flip `2.next=1`, advance `prev=2, cur=3`. Repeat: save `nxt=None`, flip `3.next=2`, advance `prev=3, cur=None`, loop ends with `head=prev=3`, giving `3→2→1→None`. You must stash `nxt` first because doing `cur.next = prev` before saving it destroys your only link to the rest of the list, orphaning everything after `cur`. The loop invariant: at the top of each iteration, `prev` heads a correctly-reversed prefix of consumed nodes and `cur` heads the untouched suffix; each iteration extends the reversed prefix by one node while shrinking the suffix by one, so when `cur` becomes `None` the suffix is empty and `prev` heads the fully reversed list, which proves correctness by induction.

column1: **Prove Floyd's.** Two pointers, +1 and +2, both inside a cycle of length `λ`. Show with the gap `d = (t - h) mod λ` that the gap shrinks by exactly 1 each step, and conclude that collision happens within `λ` steps. Why does the "speed difference of exactly 1" matter?
column2: Define the gap `d = (t - h) mod λ`, where `t` is the tortoise's position and `h` is the hare's position mod `λ`. After one step, `new gap = ((t+1) - (h+2)) mod λ = (t - h - 1) mod λ = (d - 1) mod λ`, so the gap shrinks by exactly 1 every step. Starting from some `d₀` with `0 ≤ d₀ < λ`, after exactly `d₀` steps the gap hits 0, meaning `t ≡ h (mod λ)` and they occupy the same node, so collision is guaranteed within at most `λ` steps once both pointers are in the cycle. The speed difference of exactly 1 matters because it means the hare gains one position per step relative to the tortoise and can't leap over it; it must land on it, whereas a larger speed difference (like 3x) could let the hare skip past and would need a gcd-based argument instead.

column1: **Middle in one pass.** Explain the rate argument: when fast has gone `n`, why is slow at `n/2`? What one-character change flips the even-length result from the second middle to the first?
column2: Fast moves 2 nodes per step while slow moves 1, so fast always covers exactly twice the ground slow does; when fast has traveled `n` nodes and reached the end, slow has traveled `n/2`, landing on the middle. This is purely a rate argument: fast is twice as fast, so it finishes the walk in half the steps slow needs to cover the same total distance. To flip the even-length result from the second middle to the first, start `fast = head.next` instead of `fast = head`, a one-token change noted explicitly in the chapter.

column1: **The LRU payoff.** Why does an LRU cache need a doubly linked list specifically (not singly, not an array)? Name the two operations that must be O(1) and map each to its primitive (`remove_node`, `prepend`/`add_front`, dict lookup). What role do the sentinel head/tail nodes play?
column2: An LRU cache needs a doubly linked list because "touching" an item requires unlinking an arbitrary node in O(1), which needs a `prev` pointer to splice cleanly; a singly linked list has no back-pointer so it would need an O(n) walk to find the predecessor, and an array's move-to-front would be an O(n) shift. The two operations that must be O(1) are finding an item, handled by the **dict lookup** (`key → node`), and moving/evicting it, handled by `remove_node` (O(1) unlink using the node's own `prev`/`next`) paired with `prepend`/`add_front` (O(1) reinsertion at the MRU end). The sentinel head/tail nodes are fake boundary nodes that always exist, so every real node always has real neighbors, meaning `prev`/`next` are never `None` and the code never has to special-case "is this the head/tail?", cutting down on branches and bugs.

column1: **ADT vs. implementation:** Explain why `ArrayStack` and `LinkedStack` can pass the exact same test suite despite storing data completely differently. What does the ADT promise, and what does the implementation decide?
column2: They pass identical tests because the **ADT** (Stack) is just a contract, `push`, `pop`, `peek`, `is_empty`, plus the LIFO law, that says what operations exist and what they promise, nothing about how. `ArrayStack` implements the top as the *end* of a dynamic array (cheap end for a contiguous buffer), while `LinkedStack` implements the top as the *head* of a singly linked list (cheap end for a chain), but both honor the exact same contract. The implementation is free to decide memory layout and constant factors, cache locality versus per-node pointer overhead, but as long as it satisfies the contract, it's a correct Stack.

column1: **The naive-queue trap:** Why is `list.pop(0)` O(n) while `list.pop()` is O(1)? Walk through what happens in contiguous memory for each. Then explain the two distinct fixes (ring buffer vs. linked list) and what each trades off.
column2: `list.pop(0)` is O(n) because a list is contiguous: removing index 0 leaves a hole at the front, and to keep the array contiguous every remaining element must shift one slot left, `n - 1` moves. `list.pop()` is O(1) because removing from the end just decrements `length`, no shifting required. The two fixes: a **ring/circular buffer** keeps a fixed-capacity array plus `head`/`tail` indices that wrap with modulo, giving O(1) at both ends but adding the full-vs-empty ambiguity and resize bookkeeping; a **linked list with head and tail pointers** dequeues from the head and enqueues at the tail, both O(1) worst case with no resizing, but pays per-node pointer overhead and worse cache locality since nodes are scattered.

column1: **Ring-buffer index math:** In a circular buffer of capacity `cap`, why does `(i + 1) % cap` correctly advance an index *and* handle wraparound in one expression? And why is `head == tail` ambiguous, what two states does it represent, and what are two ways to disambiguate?
column2: `(i + 1) % cap` works for both cases: if `i = cap - 1` (the last slot), `i + 1 = cap` and `cap % cap = 0`, wrapping to the front; for any `i < cap - 1`, `i + 1 < cap` so the modulo leaves it unchanged and the index just advances normally, one formula for the normal step and the wrap. `head == tail` is ambiguous because it's true both when the queue is empty (nothing stored) and when it's completely full (`tail` has wrapped all the way back around to `head`), two different states with the same index configuration that can't be told apart from `head`/`tail` alone. The two fixes are keeping an explicit `size` counter, or wasting one slot so that "full" is defined as `(tail + 1) % cap == head`.

column1: **Linked-queue invariants:** State the invariant linking `head` and `tail` in `LinkedQueue`. Identify the two edge cases that could break it and the specific lines of code that protect it.
column2: The invariant is `head is None <=> tail is None <=> size == 0`. The two edge cases are enqueueing into an empty queue, where both `head` and `tail` must be set to the new node (`if self._tail is None: self._head = node; self._tail = node`), and dequeueing the last element, where `head` becomes `None` but `tail` must also be reset (`if self._head is None: self._tail = None`) so a stale `tail` doesn't link a future enqueue onto a node that's no longer in the queue.

column1: **Stack vs. queue in the wild:** Why does DFS naturally use a stack (or recursion) while BFS uses a queue? Tie your answer to the LIFO/FIFO ordering and to why BFS finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph.
column2: DFS uses a stack (or the call stack via recursion) because when it hits a dead end it needs to back up to its most recent decision point, which is exactly LIFO: the most recently opened branch is explored first. BFS uses a queue because it explores level by level, dequeueing a node and enqueueing its unvisited neighbors, which is FIFO: nodes are visited in the order they were discovered. That FIFO discipline guarantees nodes are visited in non-decreasing distance from the start, so by the time BFS reaches any node it has already visited everything closer, which is exactly why BFS finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph.

column1: **Evaluator operand order:** In `eval_rpn`, why must the first value popped be the right operand and the second the left? Give a concrete expression where swapping them produces the wrong answer, and explain it via how operands sit on the stack.
column2: RPN preserves left-to-right operand order, so the left operand gets pushed onto the value stack first and ends up sitting underneath the right operand, which is pushed later; popping the stack therefore surfaces the right operand first and the left operand second. For `"10 6 -"`, the correct evaluation pops `right = 6`, then `left = 10`, giving `10 - 6 = 4`; swapping the order would compute `6 - 10 = -4`, which is wrong, exactly the trap the chapter's `eval_postfix` test comment ("order matters!") calls out. Because `-` and `/` are non-commutative, getting this backwards silently produces a different, incorrect result rather than an obvious error.

column1: **The monotonic pattern:** What family of problems should make you reach for a monotonic stack or deque? Explain why maintaining the stack/deque in sorted order makes "next greater element" and "sliding window maximum" run in O(n) instead of O(n²); specifically, what is the bound on how many times each element is touched?
column2: The family is "for each element, find the nearest larger or smaller element" (next greater element) or "the max/min over a sliding window" (sliding window maximum). Keeping the stack or deque in monotonic (sorted) order means each element is pushed once and popped at most once over the entire scan, a bound of a constant number of touches per element, so the total work across all `n` elements is O(n) instead of the O(n²) you'd get from comparing every element against every other. In the next-greater-element case, an element gets popped exactly when a later, bigger element resolves it; in the sliding-window-maximum case, each index enters and leaves the deque exactly once as expired or dominated indices get dropped.

column1: **Two-stack designs:** Sketch how undo/redo and browser back/forward both fall out of *two stacks plus a current item*. What single action must clear one of the stacks, and why?
column2: Both are a back/undo stack, a forward/redo stack, and a `current` item. Visiting a new page (or doing a new action) pushes `current` onto the back/undo stack and makes the new item `current`; going back pushes `current` onto the forward/redo stack and pops the back/undo stack into `current`; going forward/redo does the mirror image. The single action that must clear the forward/redo stack is visiting a new page or performing a new action, because branching off to something new makes the old forward history unreachable: once you take a new path, the old "forward" pages are gone, which is why the Forward button greys out after you click a fresh link.

column1: **Why are collisions inevitable, and why do they appear so much earlier than the table-size would suggest?** (Pigeonhole says the key universe exceeds `m` buckets so some must collide; the birthday paradox says collisions in pairs grow quadratically, so the first collision is expected after only ~`√m` insertions, not `m/2`.)
column2: Collisions are guaranteed by the **pigeonhole principle**: the universe of possible keys vastly exceeds the `m` buckets, so once more than `m` keys are inserted, some bucket must hold at least two. They show up far sooner than intuition suggests because of the **birthday paradox**: with `n` insertions there are `n(n-1)/2` pairs to compare, and that pair count grows quadratically, not linearly. The expected number of insertions before the first collision is about `1.25·√m`, so a table with `m = 1,000,000` buckets gets its first collision after roughly 1,250 insertions, not 500,000.

column1: **Walk through exactly why deleting a key in an open-addressing table needs a tombstone instead of just emptying the slot. Construct the bug.** (If `A,B,C` all probe-chain through consecutive slots and you empty `B`'s slot, a later search for `C` hits the empty slot, assumes the chain ended, and wrongly reports `C` absent. A tombstone says "keep probing" to searches while signaling "reusable" to inserts.)
column2: Deleting by simply marking a slot `EMPTY` breaks the probe chain that later searches depend on. Say `A`, `B`, `C` all hash to the same home bucket and linear probing lands them in consecutive slots, `A`@5, `B`@6, `C`@7. If you delete `B` and set slot 6 to `EMPTY`, a later `get(C)` hashes to 5 (no match), probes to 6, finds it `EMPTY`, and stops, wrongly concluding `C` isn't in the table, even though it's sitting at slot 7. The fix is a **tombstone** (`DELETED`): search treats it as keep probing, this slot was used, while insert treats it as free, reusable.

column1: **Derive the expected chain length for separate chaining, and state the analogous result for open addressing.** (Under SUHA each of `n` keys lands in a given bucket with prob `1/m`; by linearity of expectation `E[chain] = n/m = α`, so search is O(1+α). For open addressing, expected probes for an unsuccessful search ≈ `1/(1−α)`.)
column2: Under the **Simple Uniform Hashing Assumption**, each of the `n` keys lands in a given bucket independently with probability `1/m`. By **linearity of expectation**, the expected chain length in any bucket is `E[chain] = n·(1/m) = n/m = α`, so an expected search does one unit of work to hash and index plus `α` to scan the chain, giving O(1+α). For open addressing, the analogous result is that the expected number of probes for an unsuccessful search is about `1/(1−α)`, since each probe has roughly an `α` chance of hitting an occupied slot, forming a geometric-like process.

column1: **Why do we resize by *doubling*, and why doesn't the O(n) cost of a resize break our O(1) claim?** (Doubling makes resizes geometrically rarer; total resize work over `n` inserts is `1+2+4+…+n < 2n = O(n)`, so the per-insert *amortized* cost is O(1). Adding a constant amount instead would give O(n) amortized.)
column2: Doubling is chosen because it makes resizes geometrically rarer over time. If a table doubles at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, up to `n`, the total work across every resize is `1+2+4+…+n = 2n−1 = O(n)`, a geometric series that stays under `2n` even though any single resize touches all `n` entries. Spread that O(n) total cost across the `n` inserts that triggered it and the amortized cost per insert is O(1). Adding a fixed constant amount of capacity each time instead would force O(n) resizes, each O(n), giving O(n) amortized cost per insert, not O(1).

column1: **Name three situations that turn a hash table's O(1) into O(n), and how each is mitigated.** (Adversarial/colliding keys → randomized per-run hash seed; a bad/non-uniform hash function → use a good avalanching hash; unbounded load factor → resize to keep α bounded. All three break the uniform-hashing precondition the O(1) proof relies on.)
column2: Adversarial or colliding keys (hash flooding) push all inserts into one bucket or one probe run; mitigated with a randomized per-run hash seed (`PYTHONHASHSEED`) so an attacker can't predict collision sets. A bad, non-uniform hash function, like a naive one that sums character codes and collides every anagram, jams keys into a few buckets regardless of load; mitigated by using a good avalanching hash such as a polynomial rolling hash. An unbounded load factor, from never resizing, lets `α` grow without limit so chains and probe runs become O(n); mitigated by resizing to keep `α` bounded. All three break the **SUHA** precondition the O(1) proof depends on.

column1: **What probing strategy does CPython's `dict` use, and how does it avoid both primary and secondary clustering?** (Open addressing with a *perturbation* sequence roughly `j = (5j + 1 + perturb) % m`, where `perturb` is seeded from the full hash and shifted right each step, so early probes use low hash bits for cache-locality and later probes mix in high bits, making even low-bit-colliding keys diverge, avoiding the long runs of linear probing and the identical-sequence trap of quadratic probing.)
column2: CPython's `dict` uses open addressing with a **perturbation** probe sequence, roughly `j = (5*j + 1 + perturb) % m`, where `perturb` starts as the key's full hash and is shifted right each step. Early probes depend mostly on the low bits of the hash, which is fast and cache-local, while later probes mix in progressively higher bits, so even keys that collide in their low bits eventually diverge. This avoids the long contiguous runs of linear probing (**primary clustering**) and the identical-sequence problem of quadratic probing, where same-home keys repeat the same steps forever (**secondary clustering**), without needing a second full hash function like double hashing does.

column1: **A function is O(n²) because of a nested loop where the inner loop searches a list. What's the reflex to make it O(n), and name three problems it solves?** (Replace the search with an O(1) hash-map lookup, "remember what you've seen." It solves two-sum via complements, subarray-sum-equals-k via stored prefix sums, and longest-substring-without-repeats via last-seen positions.)
column2: The reflex is to replace the inner-loop search with an O(1) hash-map lookup: remember what you've seen as you scan once, instead of rescanning for each element. It solves **two-sum** by storing `value -> index` and checking whether each element's complement (`target - x`) was already seen. It solves **subarray-sum-equals-k** by storing counts of running **prefix sums** and checking for `running - k` at each step. It solves **longest-substring-without-repeating-characters** by storing the last-seen index of each character and jumping the window's left edge past a duplicate when one is found.

column1: **Depth vs. height vs. degree.** Define each precisely. For a binary tree, what's the relationship between the number of nodes `n` and the minimum possible height? What's the *maximum* possible height, and what shape causes it?
column2: **Depth** of a node is the number of edges from the root down to that node; **height** of a node is the number of edges on the longest path down to a leaf, and the height of the tree is the height of the root. **Degree** of a node is its number of children. For `n` nodes, the minimum possible height is about `⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ − 1`, achieved by a full, balanced tree where a tree of height `h` holds at most `2^(h+1) − 1` nodes. The maximum possible height is `n − 1`, caused by a degenerate tree shaped like a single chain, a linked list wearing a tree costume.

column1: **The four DFS/BFS traversals.** Give the visit order (NLR/LNR/LRN and level-order) and one real use case for each. Then explain why iterative postorder can be done as "a modified preorder, reversed": what does NRL→reverse give you, and why doesn't plain NLR→reverse work?
column2: **Preorder** (NLR) visits node, then left, then right, and is used for copying a tree since the root comes first for top-down reconstruction. **Inorder** (LNR) visits left, node, right, and on a BST prints values in sorted order. **Postorder** (LRN) visits left, right, node, and is used for deleting or freeing a tree since children are gone before their parent. **Level-order** (BFS, via a queue) visits row by row, closest nodes first. Iterative postorder works as a modified preorder reversed because an **NRL** traversal (node, right, left, produced by pushing left before right so right pops first) reversed gives **LRN**, exactly postorder; plain NLR reversed gives RLN, which puts children in the wrong relative order and isn't postorder.

column1: **BST delete, case 3.** When deleting a node with two children, why do we replace it with its inorder successor specifically, and why is deleting that successor always guaranteed to fall into the easy one-child-or-leaf case?
column2: We replace the deleted node's value with its **inorder successor**, the smallest value in its right subtree, because that's the very next value in sorted order, so dropping it into the vacated slot keeps everything to the left smaller and everything to the right larger, preserving the BST invariant. Deleting that successor is always the easy case because the successor is by definition the leftmost node of the right subtree, meaning it has no left child; it therefore has at most one child, its own right child, which is Case 1 or Case 2, so the recursion can never spiral into another two-children delete.

column1: **The balance catastrophe.** Walk through what happens when you insert `1,2,3,...,n` into a plain BST. What's the resulting height, what does that do to search complexity, and why does the BST have no defense against it?
